entries.topic: Decisions layer: the League approval of the Mandate (1922), Britain's referral to the UN (Feb 1947), Soviet support for partition (1947), the Czechoslovak arms (1948) (Nov 2026)
claims: July 1922, London: at the League Council session that approved the Mandates, Balfour spoke for Britain; he said the Mandates would operate together and appealed to Arabs and Jews to live in peace.

24 Jul 1922: the League Council confirmed the Mandate, which carried the Balfour Declaration. France held up the Palestine mandate until the Syria mandate was settled with Italy; both entered into force on 29 Sept 1923.

14 Feb 1947: the Cabinet agreed with Bevin and Creech Jones that, with neither Arabs nor Jews accepting the British plan, the question must go to the UN "without British recommendations"; Bevin announced it to the Commons on 18 Feb, citing an "irreconcilable conflict of principles".
Feb 1947: the Colonial Secretary, Arthur Creech Jones, joined Bevin in the proposal the Cabinet accepted.
Feb 1947: the Arab delegates at the London Conference rejected the British plan and any Jewish sovereignty; their refusal and the Jewish Agency's were the deadlock Bevin cited.
Feb 1947: the Jewish side sought a sovereign Jewish state and rejected the British plan.
14 May 1947: Gromyko, for the USSR, preferred one "dual, democratic" Arab-Jewish state, and called partition justifiable only if relations proved too bad for it.
By spring 1947 Stalin backed a Jewish state; the reasons reported are to get Britain out of Palestine and the hope of a pro-Soviet state.

14 Jan 1948: Foreign Minister Jan Masaryk signed the first sale: rifles, machine guns and ammunition (reported at $750,000), routed on Ethiopian papers because Czech rules allowed sales only to states.
1948: Ehud Avriel, the Haganah's man in Prague, arranged the first contract and from April 1948 bought Czech aircraft.
Avriel represented the Haganah in Prague.
